items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the insurance law, in relation to electronic delivery of property/casualty insurance notices and posting property/casualty insurance policies on the internet
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:  S2526

 TITLE OF BILL :

An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to electronic delivery
of property/casualty insurance notices and posting property/casualty
insurance policies on the internet

 PURPOSE :

To permit insurance notices and documents to be delivered
electronically with policyholder consent. To allow state-approved
insurance policies to be accessed on the internet instead of being
mailed unless specifically requested by the policyholder.

 SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS :

Section 1 adds new section 3455 to the Insurance Law. Section 3455
permits property/casualty insurers to deliver insurance notices and
documents electronically with the policyholder consent.

Section 2 adds new section 3456 to the Insurance Law. Section 3456
permits a property/casualty insurance company to elect to post
state-approved insurance policies and endorsements on the company's
website. Policyholders would be able to request a free paper copy of
the insurance policy.

Section 3 is the effective date.

 JUSTIFICATION :

Section 1: There has been an increasing trend in today's
technologically advanced society toward communicating electronically.
Insurance companies would like to provide the option to their
customers of receiving notices and documents electronically.
Currently, the Department of Financial Services has advised that the
use of electronic communications in insurance related transaction is
generally permitted, as long consumers have consented to doing
business electronically. However, there is a significant exception to
this allowance. Electronic delivery of notices is not allowed if a
statute or regulation specifically provides for a document or notice
to be "mailed." There are several statutes and regulations that still
reference delivery by "mail".

This bill would allow all insurance notices and document to be
delivered electronically as long as the consumer affirmatively
consents to receiving such notices and documents electronically. The
bill includes several safeguards designed to protect the consumer.
This includes requiring insurers to provide consumers with a clear
notice of their rights before consent is given. Consumers would have
the right to withdraw consent at any time. Before giving consent the
consumer must be provided with the hardware and software requirements
to receive documents electronically. Also, the consumer must consent
electronically in a manner that demonstrates that they can access the
information in the electronic form that will be used for electronic
document delivery. In the event the insurer makes hardware of software
change, they must notify the consumer. Any time an insurer has reason
to believe the electronic transmission has failed to reach the
consumer, they must deliver the notice or document by another delivery
method.

Section 2: Each year property and casualty insurance companies print
and then mail millions of policy contract booklets to their customers.
Often, these policies can exceed fifty pages in length.  Surveys
suggest consumers often toss their policies into the recycle bins
without ever reading them. While e-commerce laws have helped to
eliminate some of the waste, the process still has serious
limitations.

This legislation would allow the posting of standard approved
insurance policies and endorsements on the insurance company's
website, provided that the policy remains accessible for as long as
the policy is in force. Expired policies and endorsements would be
required to be available for five years, and upon request after that.

The policies and endorsements must be posted in a manner that enables
the policyholder to print and save the policy and endorsements using
programs or applications widely available on the internet and free to
use. The insurance company is required to provide with each
declaration page a description of the exact policy and endorsement
forms purchased by the insured, a description of the policyholder's
right to receive upon request and without charge, a paper copy of the
policy and endorsements by mail and the internet address where their
policy and endorsements are posted.

Personal identifying information would not be posted. This legislation
applies to insurance policy and endorsements as approved by the
Department of Financial Services.

The benefits to the insurance consumer are many. First, for the
prospective insurance buyer, he or she can look at the approved
policies and better compare the provisions of competitors. Second,
this legislation is environmentally friendly; it reduces unnecessary
and unwanted mailings. Third, there are no privacy concerns, as policy
contracts and endorsements do not contain any personal identifying
information. Fourth, electronic policy contracts create additional
features that are not possible with paper contracts, for example,
companies could augment the policies with FAQs, annotations, chat
functionality for answering questions and other content to help
consumers better understand their policies. Enabling laws have been
approved in at least thirteen other states.

 LEGISLATIVE HISTORY :

S.5249-B of 2016, passed both houses;
S.5249 of 2015, passed senate.

 FISCAL IMPLICATIONS :

None.

 EFFECTIVE DATE :
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become law.

A.memo:
BILL NUMBER: S2526A          REVISED MEMO 05/22/2018

SPONSOR: SEWARD
 
TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the insurance law, in relation to
electronic delivery of property/casualty insurance notices

 
SUMMARY OF PROVISIONS:

Section 1 adds new section 3455 to the Insurance Law. Section 3455
permits property/casualty insurers to deliver insurance notices and
documents electronically with the policyholder consent.

Section 2 establishes the effective date.

 
JUSTIFICATION:

There has been an increasing trend in today's technologically advanced
society toward communicating electronically. Insurance companies would
like to provide the option to their customers of receiving notices and
documents electronically. Currently, the Department of Financial
Services has advised that the use of electronic communications in insur-
ance related transaction is generally permitted, as long consumers have
consented to doing business electronically. However, there is a signif-
icant exception to this allowance. Electronic delivery of notices is not
allowed if a statute or regulation specifically provides for a document
or notice to be "mailed." There are several statutes and regulations
that still reference delivery by "mail".

This bill would allow all insurance notices and document to be delivered
electronically as long as the consumer affirmatively consents to receiv-
ing such notices and documents electronically. The bill includes several
safeguards designed to protect the consumer.  This includes requiring
insurers to provide consumers with a clear notice of their rights before
consent is given. Consumers would have the right to withdraw consent at
any time. Before giving consent the consumer must be provided with the

Also, the consumer must consent electronically in a manner that demon-
strates that they can access the information in the electronic form that
will be used for electronic document delivery. In the event the insurer
makes hardware of software change, they must notify the consumer. Any
time an insurer has reason to believe the electronic transmission has
failed to reach the consumer, they must deliver the notice or document
by another delivery method. The bill also adds a requirement that elec-
tronic notices provided on automobile insurance policies pursuant to
section 3425(c)(1) shall require verification or acknowledgment of
receipt of the notice.

 
LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

S.5249-B of 2016, passed both houses;
S.5249 of 2015, passed senate.

 
FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None.

 
EFFECTIVE DATE:
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall have
become law.
